u1l1.text: Insects are small animals with one thing in common: they have six legs, that is, three pairs. On the outside they have a hard skeleton, like armor, called an exoskeleton, made of chitin. Spiders have eight legs and centipedes have lots, so they are not insects. Almost all insects have wings, but some have none.

pictures.label: Centipede: many legs, not an insect

u1l2.text: An insect's body has three parts: head, thorax and abdomen. The head has the antennae, the eyes and the mouth: it is for sensing and eating. From the thorax, the middle part, come the legs below and the wings above. The abdomen, the back part, holds the heart and the digestion.

u1l3.text: All insects have three pairs of legs: six in total, and they all come out of the thorax. The wings also come out of the thorax, from the top. Most insects have two pairs of wings, but some have only one pair and others have no wings at all.

u1l4.text: Insects sense the world differently. With their antennae they pick up very faint smells in the air. For many insects, smells and tastes matter a lot: they tell them where food is and who another insect is. Their eyes are called compound eyes and have many lenses and see less than ours, but they catch movement very well, and bees see colors we can't see. Crickets hear with ears on their front legs, and grasshoppers on their abdomen. Many other insects feel sound with tiny hairs.

pictures.label: Moth: feathery antennae that pick up smells

u1l5.text: An insect's mouth is called its mouthparts, and they change depending on what it eats. Chewing mouthparts have jaws to cut and bite, like a grasshopper eating leaves. Sucking mouthparts are a tube for drinking liquids, like a butterfly drinking nectar. Piercing-sucking mouthparts pierce and suck, like a mosquito's: it bites to eat, not to attack you.

u2l1.text: There are insects almost everywhere: deserts, forests, rivers and even snowy mountains. They can live in so many places because they adapt well, are small, and many can fly. They are most common where there are green, leafy plants, because there they find leaves, seeds, fruit and nectar. Some live in fresh water and only come out when they need to breathe.

u2l2.text: Insects live a short time, so they reproduce quickly. Each one has its own trick to find a mate. Fireflies call each other with flashes of light. Male grasshoppers “sing” by rubbing their back legs against their wings. Butterflies find each other by sight, by their colors, and female moths give off a scent that males follow through the air. Bees do a dance to tell their nestmates where the flowers are, and some male beetles fight with their horns.

u2l3.text: Almost all insects start life as an egg. Complete metamorphosis has four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. A butterfly's larva is the caterpillar. Then it closes itself in a chrysalis, also called a pupa, and changes inside. Going from larva to adult can take from several weeks to years.

u2l4.text: Incomplete metamorphosis has no pupa or chrysalis: the stages are egg, nymph and adult. The young one is called a nymph, and it looks like a miniature version of its parents, usually without wings. To grow, the nymph sheds its exoskeleton when it gets too small: this is called molting. This is how a grasshopper grows, for example.

u3l1.text: Butterflies and moths are lepidopterans, which means “scaly wings”: their wings are covered with tiny colored scales. As adults they have a coiled proboscis that stretches like a straw to drink nectar. Antennae help tell them apart: butterflies' end in a little knob, while moths' usually look like feathers or threads. Their caterpillars have jaws to chew leaves. They have complete metamorphosis, pollinate flowers (carry pollen from one flower to another) and are food for birds.

u3l2.text: Beetles, ladybugs and fireflies are coleopterans, which means “sheathed wings”. Their front wings are hard and are called elytra: like a case, they protect the thin wings they fly with. They have chewing mouths to bite leaves, wood or small prey. They are the animal group with the most species in the world, and many are nature's recyclers.

u3l3.text: Bees, wasps and ants are hymenopterans, which means “membrane wings”. A membrane is a thin, see-through skin. Bees have two pairs of wings like that, and ants are their cousins. Many live in groups and share the work. Bees pollinate flowers, and that's why we have fruit. Wasps hunt other insects that harm plants, and they pollinate too. A bee or a wasp only stings to defend itself or its nest: if one flies near you, stay still and calm, and it will leave.

u3l4.text: Dragonflies and damselflies are odonates. They have four long, narrow, clear wings with veins like a net, and they move them separately: that's why they fly so well. They are hunters and catch mosquitoes in flight, but they don't bite people. Their nymphs grow underwater, and if a river has many dragonflies, the water is clean.

u3l5.text: Grasshoppers, crickets and locusts are orthopterans, which means “straight wings”. Their back legs are big, like springs, for jumping. They have chewing mouths to bite leaves and grow by incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph and adult. They are food for birds, frogs and lizards.

u3l6.text: Stink bugs, cicadas and aphids are hemipterans, which means “half wing”, because in true bugs the front wings are half hard and half thin. What they all share is the mouth: it's like a needle to pierce plants and suck their juice, the sap. Many stink bugs give off a strong smell to defend themselves, and male cicadas sing very loudly on hot days. If you see a stink bug, look at it without touching it.

u3l7.text: Flies and mosquitoes are dipterans, which means “two wings”: they have only one pair of wings. Their larvae have no legs. They have a bad reputation, but many flies do an important job: they break down remains and clean up nature, and some also pollinate flowers.

u4l1.text: Insects help us a lot. Pollinating means carrying pollen from one flower to another so there are fruits and seeds, and bees, butterflies and many flies do it. Others, like beetles, are recyclers: they turn remains into rich soil. If insects disappeared, we would run out of fruit and many birds would go hungry.

u4l2.text: A pest is when there are huge numbers of one kind of insect damaging crops or food, like aphids or weevils. If we spray insecticide everywhere, bees, ladybugs and other helpers die too. Biological control is better: using their natural enemies, like the ladybug, which eats hundreds of aphids. And keeping food in tightly closed jars prevents pests without poison.

u4l3.text: A few insects can sting or carry diseases. They are not evil: they do what they need to live. Only female mosquitoes bite, because they need blood to lay their eggs, and they lay them in still water: that's why we empty buckets, tires and flower vases. If a bee stings you and it swells a lot or you find it hard to breathe, tell an adult right away. Don't touch bugs that can spread disease: if you see one at home, tell an adult.

u4l4.text: Today you review everything. Some insects are harmless, like the butterfly, the ladybug or the dragonfly, which doesn't bite and eats mosquitoes. Others can be harmful, meaning they can damage crops or food when there are huge numbers, like locusts or weevils. And with others it's best to be careful because they can sting or make you ill, like the mosquito, the bee or the kissing bug. A good forest ranger observes them, respects them and stays safe without wiping them out.

u5l1.text: Venezuela has many landscapes: plains, mountains, rainforest, coast and islands. The plains (los llanos) are flat, hot grasslands; in the rainy season they fill with ponds, and dragonfly and mosquito young grow in the water. The Andes have cold mountains with páramo, where fuzzy bumblebees visit the flowers of the frailejón plant. In the rainforest it rains a lot, the trees are very tall and the blue morpho flies. On the coast and the islands it is hot and it rarely rains. Each landscape has its own living things: that great variety of life is called biodiversity, and because Venezuela has so much of it, it is one of the few megadiverse countries in the world.

u5l2.text: The cocuyo is a beetle that makes light. The firefly is also a beetle and also makes light, but they are not the same (in many places people call fireflies cocuyos, too). The cocuyo has two green lights on its thorax, like two headlights, and when it flies an orange light shows underneath, on its belly. The firefly, on the other hand, lights up the tip of its abdomen and makes it blink. Making light with the body is called bioluminescence, and it is cold light: it doesn't burn. Before there was electric light, people used cocuyos to light their way at night: with several together you could see the path.

u5l3.text: The blue morpho is a big butterfly with bright blue wings. That blue isn't paint: the scales on its wings have a tiny shape that bounces back blue light, like the colors that shine on a soap bubble. Underneath, its wings are brown with circles that look like eyes: when it closes them it hides, and the “eyes” confuse birds that want to eat it. The 88 butterfly is small and has an 88 drawn under its back wings. The monarch, orange and black, also lives in Venezuela; in North America, monarchs travel thousands of miles every year to escape the cold, and that is called migrating.

u5l4.text: The angelita is a very small bee from here: its stinger is so tiny that it doesn't work, so it can't sting. It lives in a group inside holes in trees or walls, and the entrance to its nest is a little wax tube. It makes a much-loved honey, which many people use as a home remedy, and it pollinates flowers in forests and small farms. The bachaco is a big leafcutter ant that cuts little pieces of leaf and carries them in a line to its underground nest. It doesn't eat the leaves: it uses them to grow a fungus, and that fungus is its food. Leafcutter ants are farmers! They can bite hard with their jaws, so it's best to watch them from a distance, without putting your hand in their line or their nest.

u5l5.text: The Hercules beetle lives in Venezuela's humid forests and is one of the biggest beetles in the world: counting its horn, it can be longer than your hand! Only the males have horns, and they use them to push other males, not to attack people. The stick insect looks like a twig: it stays still or sways slowly, like a branch moved by the wind, so birds don't see it. The praying mantis is green or brown like leaves, has a triangle-shaped head and waits very still, with its front legs folded as if it were praying. Those legs have little spines and snap shut fast to catch flies and mosquitoes. None of the three stings or has venom.

pictures.label: Stick insect: looks like a twig

u5l6.text: Venezuela's insects are in danger when forests are cut down or burned, because they lose their home and their food. Poison sprayed on plants also harms them, because it doesn't kill only pests: it also kills bees, butterflies and ladybugs. To protect them, Venezuela has national parks, places where nature is protected by law. Canaima, in the south, has tepuis (flat-topped mountains) and Angel Falls, the highest waterfall in the world. Henri Pittier, in Aragua, was the country's first national park, and every year huge numbers of insects and birds fly through its Portachuelo pass. You can help too: plant flowers, don't use poison, leave insects free and teach others not to be afraid of them.

u6l1.text: Insects have cousins: spiders, scorpions, centipedes, millipedes and pill bugs. Together they make up one big family, the arthropods, which means “jointed legs”: their legs bend in sections, like your fingers. They all have their skeleton on the outside, hard armor that can't stretch, so to grow they swap it for a new one: that's molting, or shedding. To tell who's who, count legs: insects have 6; spiders and scorpions, 8 (a scorpion's pincers aren't legs); the pill bug, 14; and centipedes and millipedes, lots and lots. Frogs, birds and we also have a skeleton, but on the inside: we aren't arthropods.

pictures.label: Centipede: lots and lots of legs

u6l2.text: Spiders aren't insects: they're arachnids. They have 8 legs, a body in 2 parts (the cephalothorax in front, where the legs come out, and the abdomen behind) and no antennae or wings, while insects have 6 legs, 3 parts and antennae. All spiders make silk in their abdomen and let it out through the spinnerets, tiny tubes at the tip, but not all of them spin webs: some hunt by jumping or running. A web is a trap with sticky threads: when an insect gets caught, the spider feels the thread shake with its legs. Almost all spiders are harmless to people and eat mosquitoes, flies and cockroaches: they guard our homes and gardens!

u6l3.text: Almost all spiders are so small, or have such weak venom, that they can't harm a person; they're also shy and only bite if they're squashed or grabbed. In Venezuela there are a few that can be dangerous, like the black widow (shiny black with red marks) and the recluse spider (brown, it hides in dark places and in clothes that are put away). Those, and any spider you don't know, are watched from a distance and you tell an adult. If a spider is inside the house, an adult can cover it with a glass, slide a piece of card underneath and let it go outside, among the plants. So you don't get a fright, shake out shoes and stored clothes before putting them on, look before you put your hand into a dark corner and, if you see a web, look at it without breaking it. And if a spider ever bites you, tell an adult right away.

u6l4.text: Centipedes and millipedes are myriapods, which means “many legs”. They have a long body made of many rings (segments) and two antennae on their head. The centipede is fast and a hunter: it has one pair of legs on each ring and goes out at night to hunt insects with venomous claws next to its mouth; its bite hurts, so you watch it from a distance. The millipede is slow and calm: it has two pairs of legs on almost every ring, eats dead leaves and rotting wood, and when it's scared it curls up like a snail shell. Despite their names, a centipede has between 30 and more than 300 legs, but never exactly one hundred, and almost no millipede reaches a thousand.

u6l5.text: The pill bug, or roly-poly, isn't an insect: it's a crustacean, a cousin of shrimp and crabs. It has 14 legs and breathes with special gills that must stay damp, so it lives in damp, dark places, like under stones and flowerpots. It eats dead leaves and plant scraps and turns them into soil: it's a recycler, and when it's scared it rolls into a ball to protect itself with its armor. The scorpion is an arachnid, a cousin of spiders: it has 8 legs, two pincers in front and a tail with a stinger at the tip, and it goes out at night to hunt insects. Some scorpions in Venezuela have strong venom, especially for children: watch them from a distance, tell an adult and shake out your shoes before putting them on. If one stings you, tell an adult right away so you can go to the doctor.

u6l6.text: To tell whether a critter is an insect or a cousin, count its legs and its parts. Insects have 6 legs, 3 parts (head, thorax and abdomen) and two antennae, and many have wings. Arachnids, like the spider and the scorpion, have 8 legs, 2 parts and no antennae. Myriapods, like the centipede and the millipede, have lots and lots of legs and a body made of rings; the pill bug, with 14 legs, is a crustacean. Many insects sing, like the cricket, which rubs its wings; a frog, on the other hand, croaks with an air sac in its throat and is an amphibian, with its skeleton on the inside. They all have a job: some hunt bugs, like the spider, and others recycle dead leaves, like the millipede and the pill bug.

u7l1.text: A food chain tells who eats whom. It always starts with a plant, which makes its own food from sunlight. Next comes whoever eats the plant, like the caterpillar that chews leaves, and then whoever eats the caterpillar, like the bird that takes it to its chicks. Lots of animals eat insects: frogs catch them with their sticky tongues, lizards and praying mantises hunt them by day, and bats hunt them at night. Frogs sing (croak) near water, especially at dusk. A grown-up butterfly, on the other hand, doesn't hunt: it drinks nectar from flowers.

u7l2.text: A flower has several parts. The brightly colored petals and the flower's scent attract insects from far away. The stamens are thin threads that hold the pollen, a yellow dust, and in the middle is the pistil: at its base the fruit and the seeds will grow. The bee goes in to drink nectar, a sweet juice, and to collect pollen for its young, and the pollen sticks to the little hairs on its body. When it visits another flower of the same kind, some pollen falls on the pistil: that's pollination, and that's how the flower can turn into a fruit with seeds. The stem holds the flower up and brings it water.

u7l3.text: Every day, leaves, branches, fruit and dead animals fall in the forest. Recyclers eat those leftovers and break them into smaller and smaller pieces: that's called decomposing. Some recyclers are insects, like many beetles, fly larvae, ants and termites, which eat wood. Fungi and earthworms recycle too, but they aren't insects: a fungus isn't even an animal, and an earthworm is a worm. In the end, the leftovers turn into new soil, full of food for plants. Without recyclers, the forest would be covered in mountains of dry leaves.

u7l4.text: Many insects escape from whoever wants to eat them without having to fight. With camouflage they look like their surroundings: the stick insect looks like a twig, the praying mantis blends in with the leaves (that's also how it surprises the insects it hunts) and some caterpillars stay stiff like a branch. With mimicry they dress up as another animal: the flower fly has yellow and black stripes like a wasp, but it doesn't sting. Some tasty butterflies copy the colors of others that taste bad, so birds leave them alone. Other insects do the opposite and show off warning colors, like the ladybug's red with black spots, which says “I taste bad, don't eat me”.

u7l5.text: Some insects live in big families called colonies: honey bees, ants and termites. In the colony there is a queen who lays the eggs (termites also have a king) and lots and lots of workers who look for food, care for the young and clean the nest. Some ants and termites also have soldiers, with big heads, who defend the nest. Each one does its part, and together they achieve what none could alone, like the bees' honeycomb or the termites' huge nests. The leafcutter ant cuts leaves, but it doesn't eat them: it carries them to the nest to grow a fungus, which is its food. Some ants protect aphids from their enemies, and in return the aphids give them sweet little drops.

pictures.label: Colony with a queen and a king

u7l6.text: All the threads of the web are tied together: if one breaks, the others feel it. Without insect pollinators there would be very few mangoes, passion fruits and watermelons, and no chocolate at all: cacao flowers are pollinated by tiny midges. Corn and rice, on the other hand, don't need insects: the wind carries their pollen. Without recyclers, leftovers would pile up and the soil would run out of food for plants. Without insects, many birds, frogs and bats would go hungry, because many birds feed their chicks with insects. To help them, we can plant flowers, not spray poison everywhere and leave a corner with dry leaves in the garden.

u8l1.text: Scientists start by observing: looking calmly, quietly and without hurrying. A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger, but never hold it in the sun over an insect: it focuses the light and can burn it. In a field notebook you write the date, the place and what the insect is doing, and you draw what you see. To measure without touching, you place a ruler next to the insect, and a watch tells you how long you observed. You also observe with your ears: a cricket sings by rubbing its wings together.

pictures.label: Magnifying glass: makes small things bigger

u8l2.text: After observing, a scientist asks a question that can be checked by looking or counting, like “Which flower do bees visit most?”. Questions like “Which insect is the prettiest?” can't be checked, because it depends on each person's taste. Then they make a hypothesis: what they think will happen, and why. Next they check it: they observe, count and write down the results. At the end they draw a conclusion: what they learned. If the hypothesis was wrong, that's okay!: you still learn, and a new question comes up.

u8l3.text: An experiment is a way to check a hypothesis. To make it fair, you change only one thing and keep everything else the same: for example, counting for 5 minutes at each flower, at the same time of day. Bees see blue, purple and yellow very well, but red looks dark to them. Pill bugs need damp to breathe, so they are usually in the shade, under leaves and stones. In a good experiment insects are not caught or shut in: you observe them where they are and leave everything as it was.

u8l4.text: An insect hotel is a shelter made of natural things: hollow canes, pine cones, twigs, bark and wood with holes. In the canes, solitary bees make their nests: each mother leaves her eggs with pollen and seals the entrance with mud or bits of leaf. They live alone, with no hive to defend, so they almost never sting; ladybugs shelter among the pine cones and bark. Mosquitoes and dragonflies don't use it, because their young grow up in water. The hotel goes where it gets the morning sun, sheltered from the rain, at least three feet off the ground and near flowers.

u8l5.text: Insects have a hard time where there is poison, trash, few plants or too much heat. Poison sprayed all over the garden doesn't just kill pests: it also kills the bees and ladybugs that help us. Lights left on at night confuse moths and fireflies, which look for each other with their own light. When the planet warms up, some flowers and puddles dry out, and insects have less food and water. The good news is that small actions help!: planting flowers, leaving a corner with wild plants and dry leaves, not spraying everything, picking up trash and turning off lights that aren't being used.

pictures.label: Looks for others with its light

u8l6.text: An expert forest ranger does four things: observes, respects, cares and teaches. They observe calmly, with their notebook, like a scientist. They respect: they don't catch or squash, and they leave each insect in its home; they care: they plant flowers, don't use poison and turn off lights that aren't being used. They teach: they help others not to be afraid, telling them that almost all insects are harmless and it's enough to watch them from a distance. If an insect gets into the house, you take it out with a cup and a piece of cardboard and let it go outside; if it's one that stings, you tell an adult.
